title: SpaceX IPO Reveals Who Bet Biggest on Musk's Space Empire
excerpt: From Alphabet's $900 million check in 2015 to Founders Fund's $20 million bet that turned into $50 billion, the largest IPO in history has exposed the investors behind SpaceX's $2 trillion valuation.
body:
• Elon Musk holds roughly 42% of SpaceX equity worth over $1 trillion, with a lockup preventing any sales until June 2027
  • Alphabet is the largest outside shareholder at ~7%, tracing back to a $900 million investment in 2015 alongside Fidelity
  • Founders Fund's $20 million Series C bet in 2008 is now worth approximately $50 billion — one of the greatest venture returns ever
  • SpaceX's dual-class share structure gives Musk 82.4% of voting power, effectively making public shareholders passengers on his rocket

SpaceX's June 2026 IPO — priced at $135 per share and raising $75 billion — was the largest public offering in history. It floated just 4.3% of the company's equity, but it cracked open the ownership map of a $2 trillion enterprise that had been private for two decades. The names behind it range from Silicon Valley legends to a mutual-fund manager who became one of Elon Musk's most vocal cheerleaders.

Musk's Trillion-Dollar Lockup

There is no contest at the top. Musk holds close to 42% of SpaceX's equity — roughly 850 million Class A shares and 5.6 billion Class B shares — a stake worth more than $1 trillion at the IPO valuation. An additional billion Class B shares are contingent on a million people living in a SpaceX colony on Mars, a provision that is simultaneously audacious and unserious. He can vote those shares now.

Musk's entire block sits under a lockup that expires in June 2027 with no early release provision. The largest holder is a seller of nothing for the company's first year on public markets.

The Outside Shareholders

Behind Musk, the biggest holder is a name many investors overlook. Alphabet, the parent of Google, owns close to 7% of SpaceX — a position that traces back to a $1 billion investment it made alongside Fidelity in January 2015. Alphabet put in $900 million; Fidelity contributed the remaining $100 million. That single check turned a search-advertising company into the largest outside shareholder of a rocket maker.

"The AI earnings-driven tech boom continues. It's an earnings boom, not a bubble."

— Jay Hatfield, CEO, Infrastructure Capital Advisors

Antonio Gracias, a board member and founder of Valor Equity Partners, holds 503.4 million shares — a position valued at nearly $68 billion at the IPO price. Gracias has backed multiple Musk ventures and is one of his closest confidants. SpaceX board member Luke Nosek owns 33 million shares, while COO Gwynne Shotwell — who has led the company's daily operations for over 20 years — holds 12.6 million shares.

Venture Capital's Greatest Hits

The early venture backers hold the most striking returns rather than the largest slices. Founders Fund, the firm co-founded by Peter Thiel, wrote a $20 million check in SpaceX's 2008 Series C round. That stake is now worth $50 billion — a 2,500x return that ranks among the most lucrative venture bets in history. Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, and Valor Equity Partners each hold positions of around 2% or below.

The February 2026 merger with xAI added new names to the register, including Nvidia and the Qatar Investment Authority, a sovereign wealth fund. Among hedge funds, Darsana Capital Partners — which first invested in SpaceX in 2019 — holds a stake that could be worth over $10 billion. Ron Baron, the 83-year-old mutual-fund manager, has also bet heavily on the company.

A Dual-Class Power Structure

Buying SpaceX stock makes you an owner of the economics, but it does not give you a voice. The company uses a dual-class structure: Musk's Class B shares carry 10 votes each, giving him 82.4% of total voting power. Public shareholders who buy Class A stock gain exposure to the rocket and satellite business without any real say in how it is run.

"The dual-class share structure effectively entrenches Musk as a CEO who can't be deposed."

— Lindsey Stewart, Director, Morningstar

Morningstar has flagged the governance structure as one of the most investor-unfriendly among major public companies. SpaceX qualifies as a "controlled company" exempt from certain corporate governance requirements, including fully independent committees for nominating directors or setting executive compensation.

The Public Float Is Small — For Now

The IPO floated less than 5% of the equity, leaving 95% in the hands of insiders, early investors, and employees who have waited years for tender offers. Institutional buyers like Invesco (0.76% stake) and Vanguard (0.46%) have begun building positions, and more shares will reach the market as lockups expire through late 2026 and 2027.

SpaceX, trading under the ticker SPCX, closed at roughly $148-$152 in recent sessions. Analysts on TipRanks have assigned an average price target of $243.81, implying over 100% upside from the IPO price. The stock carries a Strong Buy consensus based on 23 Buy ratings, five Holds, and one Sell. Whether the valuation — which assumes almost everything goes right — justifies the ride is up to each investor to decide.
nri_angle: Indian-American venture capitalists and tech investors are among those with exposure to SpaceX through VC funds and ETFs that now hold SPCX shares.
